alerts.title: Carbamazepine-DTG interaction lowers DTG levels
alerts.message: Guidelines state carbamazepine decreases DTG levels by 30–70% and recommend using valproic acid instead. Patient started carbamazepine 2 weeks ago while on DTG-based TLD. Viral load rose from <50 copies/mL (Sep 2025) to 1,240 copies/mL today, with adherence reported good. This temporal relationship strongly suggests the interaction caused subtherapeutic DTG levels leading to virologic breakthrough. The patient is already on valproate, which the guidelines specifically recommend as the alternative antiepileptic. Carbamazepine toxicity (level 14 mcg/mL, hyponatremia, ataxia, nystagmus) provides further reason to discontinue it.

evidence.recommended_action: Stop carbamazepine and manage seizures with valproate monotherapy as guidelines recommend. Repeat viral load after discontinuation to assess DTG level recovery.

alerts.title: Detectable viral load requires enhanced adherence counseling
alerts.message: Guidelines define treatment failure as two consecutive viral load results >1,000 copies/mL. For high-level viremia ≥1,000, guidelines require intensive adherence counseling (IAC) with 3 sessions scoring >95%, CD4 testing, and repeat viral load using two plasma samples. If repeat remains ≥1,000, HIV drug resistance testing and regimen switching are indicated. Patient's viral load is 1,240 copies/mL today, up from <50 in September 2025. The clinician's plan does not mention IAC, CD4 testing, or repeat VL protocol. The likely cause is the carbamazepine-DTG interaction, but the full guideline workup should still be initiated.

evidence.recommended_action: Initiate IAC sessions, conduct CD4 testing, and repeat viral load with two plasma samples. If still ≥1,000, perform HIV drug resistance testing and consider regimen switch.

alerts.title: Carbamazepine toxicity with hyponatremia
alerts.message: Patient has carbamazepine level 14 mcg/mL (therapeutic 4–12), with clinical features of toxicity including ataxia, horizontal nystagmus, fine tremor, dizziness, and headaches. Hyponatremia (sodium 128 mmol/L) is also present and is a known adverse effect of carbamazepine. ALT 68 U/L may reflect hepatic effects of carbamazepine, valproate, or both antiepileptics together. The clinician plans dose reduction, but given the concurrent DTG interaction and the guideline recommendation to use valproic acid instead, simply reducing the dose may not address the underlying interaction driving virologic failure.

evidence.recommended_action: Discontinue carbamazepine rather than dose-reducing, given DTG interaction and toxicity. Monitor sodium, ALT, and neurological symptoms after withdrawal. Consider valproate monotherapy optimization.

alerts.title: Carbamazepine-valproate hepatotoxicity risk
alerts.message: Patient is on two hepatotoxic antiepileptics simultaneously: carbamazepine and valproate. ALT is elevated at 68 U/L. Guidelines note that co-administration of interacting medicines increases the likelihood of toxicities, and recommend liver function tests based on clinical indication. The dual antiepileptic regimen compounds hepatotoxicity risk. While the ALT elevation is modest, continued co-prescription without hepatic monitoring could lead to progressive liver injury. Carbamazepine discontinuation (already recommended for the DTG interaction) would reduce this risk.

evidence.recommended_action: Perform baseline and follow-up liver function tests. Discontinue carbamazepine to eliminate the interaction and reduce hepatic burden. Recheck ALT after withdrawal.

Consolidated Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of HIV and Aids in Uganda - 2022 virological monitoring provides an early and more accurate indication of treatment failure and indicates the need to switch from first line to second-line drugs, and from second- line to third-line drugs, toward reducing accumulation of drug-resistance mutations and improved clinical outcomes. Dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens (e.g., tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir [TLD]) have increased viral load suppression (VLS) rates to unprecedented levels, hence a need to actively monitor patients for low-level viremia to keep DTG a durable treatment option for as long as possible. Furthermore, low-level viraemia monitoring can enhances monitoring of achieving and sustaining HIV epidemic control, as viral load of >200 copies/mL is associated with potential risk of sexual transmission as well as subsequent virologic non-suppression and treatment failure.

Given the above background and taking into consider the 2021 World Health Organization guidance to monitor low-level viremia, the guidelines have been designed to carter for health facilities with capacity to utilize plasma and dried blood spot (DBS) samples at suppression cut off points of 200 copies/ mL and 400 copies/mL respectively, as shown in Figure 58. A patient who has been on ART for more than 6 months and is responding to ART is considered virally suppressed at VL <200 copies/mL and <400 copies/mL for plasma and DBS samples, respectively. Facilities should constitute a multidisciplinary VL review committees to review, track, and make decisions to optimize ART regimen by switching to second-line, third- line, or a more potent regimen. At the minimum, the committee should consist of a healthcare worker and a lay provider (e.g. expert client, counselor, peer education, VHT) who knows the client. ## 6.12.3 Frequency of viral load monitoring

Consolidated Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of HIV and Aids in Uganda - 2022 ## 6.5 FIRST-LINE ART REGIMENS FOR PATIENTS INITIATING ART Principles for selecting the ARV regimens (treatment optimization): The first-line ART regimens for treating HIV infection in Uganda were selected based on the universal principles: * Toxicity: regimens with less toxicity are preferred. * Palatability and pill burden; better palatability and lower pill burden preferred. * Increased durability and efficacy. * Sequencing: spares other available formulations for use in the 2nd line regimen. * Harmonization of regimen across age and population. * Lower cost.
